newsitem.title: UK: Emerging market Eurobond price collapse continues.
newsitem.headline: Emerging market Eurobond price collapse continues.

text.p: Emerging market Eurobond prices have continued to decline amid expectations of a U.S. interest rate rise and will keep falling while U.S. Treasuries remain unsettled, dealers said on Tuesday.
"As long as the market feels Treasuries have not found a stable level and may go down, people will not be comfortable buying emerging market assets," a senior debt trader at a U.S. bank said.
Mexico's 2026 global dollar bond, a benchmark for the sector, was trading 380 basis points over the U.S. long bond, up from a 315 b.p. yield spread early last Thursday, dealers said.
Emerging market debt selling was triggered by comments from U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan that the Fed could tighten monetary policy before evidence of inflation emerged.
Markets now expect U.S. interest rates to go up, perhaps as early as the March 25 Federal Open Market Committee meeting.
U.S. employment data for February, due to be released on Friday, will be closely watched for signs of economic growth and wage pressures, dealers said.
"Emerging markets are looking at the Treasury market for direction, and non-farm payrolls on Friday will be pretty important," a dealer at another U.S. bank said.

But the year's gains have not yet been completely wiped out. J.P. Morgan's composite emerging market bond index closed on Monday at 147.01, down from last Tuesday's peak of 153.30. The index ended 1996 at 143.17.
Similarly, J.P. Morgan's index of Latin American Eurobonds was down to 175.50 from 179.86 last Tuesday. At the end of December these bonds stood at 171.36.
"Generally speaking emerging market assets have been on a very long bull run for the past 15 months," an emerging market debt trader at a European bank said.

"That has caused the market to appear to re-assess the risk of owning these assets. Indeed, the risks are now lower because fundamentally these countries are safer places to put your money in. But the improvement in spreads (this year) has been far greater than the fundamentals justify," he said.
He added the recent sell-off triggered by changes in interest-rate views rather than a change in perception of emerging market credits.

"Money goes wherever the next hot market is, and emerging markets have been the hot market for a while. Now we have to bear the consequences of attracting this money by seeing it leave the market," the trader said.
Emerging market borrowers have taken advantage of the huge appetite for their debt by issuing record amounts of bonds.
More than $12 billion was launched by Latin American names by February 21, a recent ING Barings report said. Most of this came from sovereign borrowers, which raised nearly $8.0 billion.
